newsitem.title: UK: European stocks seek guidance as Wall St holidays.
newsitem.headline: European stocks seek guidance as Wall St holidays.

text.p: European share markets groped for direction on Monday, deprived of guidance from Wall Street which has led them on a bull run since the New Year.

Leading European markets all slipped with U.S. markets closed for the President's Day holiday on Monday, but some dealers said a modest consolidation after the recent record runs would be no bad thing.

The foreign exchange market also lacked inspiration due to the U.S. holiday, with the dollar still firm against the mark but down from Asian highs against the yen as unease grows that the Bank of Japan might mount a surprise intervention.
British, German and French stocks were all lower by late morning following a weaker Friday close on Wall Street before the long U.S. holiday weekend.
"Wall Street has been one of the main things driving us along and that's closed today," one London trader said. "We're unlikely to want to go too much higher on our own."
Deprived of action, dealers began to wonder how long the New Year bull run, inspired by Wall Street, could last.
"Some people are trying to call the top (of the market)," one said. "With the Dow going above 7,000 and then closing below it, some people there are a little more pessimistic."
In London, the FTSE 100 index was down 16.3 points at 4,324.7 at late morning after closing at a record on Friday.

Investors suffered the additional twin worries of a strong sterling, which hurts British exporters, and a parliamentary vote scheduled for Monday night which is aimed at bringing down the Conservative government.
"Nobody likes this kind of instability," one dealer said.
"Sterling has been a constant worry but the worry hasn't been going away and we could see it hurting again today."

The opposition Labour Party will try to bring down the government with a vote expected around 2200 GMT on whether to censure Agriculture Minister Douglas Hogg over his handling of the Mad Cow disease crisis.
If Prime Minister John Major lost, there could be a confidence vote in the government the next day. If he lost that vote, Major would have call an early general election.
However, Monday's vote is likely to be little more than a nagging worry as Major is expected to win it narrowly and he has to call an election by May in any case.

German stocks likewise fell, with dealers citing profit taking after 11 consecutive record closes plus Friday's losses on Wall Street, where the Dow Jones Industrial average closed down 33.48 points at 6,988.96.
The DAX index was down 12.03 points at 3,236.15 at late morning and German dealers welcomed the drop.
"Everyone here is hoping that the market will fall back so that taking new positions will be cheaper. After 11 record days a breathing space will do nothing but good," said one.

Profit takers also stalked the Paris market, with the CAC 40 index down 7.6 at 2,619.82. Car maker Renault recovered some early losses but was still down 2.61 percent at 119.3 francs after warning last week that its losses would be worse than the market expected.

On the foreign exchange markets, the dollar was buoyant against the mark and Swiss franc, but below overnight highs against the yen, weakened by a Tokyo report that Japan would intervene alone if the yen fell sharply.
